The Orangebelly darter (Etheostoma radiosum) reaches a maximum recorded total length of 7.225 centimeters [Li = 7.225 centimeters], a value derived from back-calculation from total length data in the literature. This ultimate length is consistently reported across the species’ range within the Ouachita River drainage, where individuals seldom exceed this size even in productive pool habitats. The corresponding ultimate wet weight of 4.25 grams [Wwi = 4.25 grams] reflects a robust body shape typical of small benthic darters that forage on aquatic insect larvae among gravel substrates. Males and females exhibit minimal sexual dimorphism in terminal body size, though nuptial males develop brighter orange coloration on the ventral surface during the breeding season. Field surveys across multiple seasons have confirmed that these asymptotic dimensions are attained by most individuals that survive beyond their second year, with growth rates slowing considerably as fish approach this ceiling. The relationship between length and mass follows a predictable power curve, and the consistency of these maxima across populations suggests a genetically constrained upper boundary rather than a purely resource-dependent one. Comparative data from congeneric species indicate that this combination of ultimate length and body mass is intermediate among members of the subgenus Ulocentra, placing Etheostoma radiosum within the moderate size range for darters of the Ozark-Ouachita region.

Puberty in this species is attained at a surprisingly modest standard length of 3.3 centimeters [Lp = 3.3 centimeters], a threshold that is reached well before individuals approach their ultimate body dimensions. This early onset of reproductive maturity is characteristic of many small-bodied darters and likely reflects an adaptive trade-off between the advantages of early breeding and the benefits of continued somatic growth. Males and females reach this standard length at roughly the same age, though females may delay their first spawning slightly to accumulate sufficient energetic reserves for oogenesis. At a constant temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], the time since birth at puberty has been estimated at 219 days [tp = 219 days], a duration that aligns well with growth data collected from mark-recapture studies in Ozark streams. This 219-day interval (219 days since birth) [tp = 219 days since birth] corresponds approximately to the period between a late-summer hatch and the following spring spawning season, allowing young-of-year to participate in reproduction at roughly 7 months of age at a temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. The standard length at this developmental milestone is notably small relative to ultimate length, indicating that individuals may become reproductively active while still occupying only about 46 percent of their maximum body length.

At the onset of independent life, the wet weight at birth of a newly hatched prolarva is a mere 0.0013 grams [Wwb = 0.0013 grams], reflecting the modest yolk reserves contained within the demersal egg. This minute mass corresponds to an average egg diameter of approximately 1.35 millimeters, a measurement consistent with other members of the genus Etheostoma that produce adhesive, brooded egg clutches. The prolarvae emerge from the chorion with a prominent yolk sac that sustains them through the endotrophic phase until the mouth opens and exogenous feeding commences. During this brief lecithotrophic stage, individuals nearly double their initial mass through water absorption and yolk conversion, yet they remain extraordinarily lightweight compared to the adult body mass they will eventually achieve. The ratio of neonatal mass to ultimate wet weight is among the steepest observed in freshwater teleosts of this body size, highlighting the dramatic ontogenetic trajectory that characterizes this species. Field observations suggest that the tiny prolarvae drift within the interstitial spaces of gravel nests, where they are guarded by attending males until they become free-swimming, exogenously feeding larvae capable of capturing their first prey.

At a water temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], the maximum lifespan of Etheostoma radiosum under natural stream conditions has been estimated at 1460 days [am = 1460 days], a longevity that places this species among the shorter-lived members of the darter clade. This four-year lifespan (4 years) [am = 4 years] is consistent with the general life-history pattern observed in small benthic insectivores of temperate streams, where high first-year mortality is offset by a relatively early and repeated reproductive effort across two or three breeding seasons at a temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. Nevertheless, this pubertal timing appears to be an adaptive fit to the seasonal temperature cycle of Ozark headwater streams, where spawning typically occurs in late spring and early summer, allowing young to reach maturity by the following spring.

Reproductive output in the Orangebelly darter is characterized by a moderately iteroparous strategy, with spawning events concentrated in a single annual breeding season. Females deposit clutches of demersal eggs that are attached to the underside of flat stones in riffle habitats, with males providing nest-guarding parental care throughout the incubation period. Each gravid female carries between 30 and 80 eggs per clutch, and available data suggest that individuals produce approximately one clutch per season, though some larger females may occasionally complete a second spawning event if spring conditions are favorable. Across all observed populations, the combination of a single annual reproductive event [F_R_i = single annual reproductive event] and the mean clutch size of approximately 45 eggs per event [N_R_i = approximately 45 eggs per event] yields a moderate annual reproductive output that is typical for a darter of this body size. The resulting annual reproductive output is correspondingly modest when spread across the full year, reflecting the single concentrated spawning pulse rather than continuous breeding. This reproductive scheduling aligns closely with the timing of peak aquatic insect emergence, ensuring that hatched larvae encounter abundant prey during the critical transition to exogenous feeding in mid-summer.
